payload.rationale: The contract requires the 2026 NASA GISS LOTI anomaly to exceed both the 2025 value and 1.28°C. GISS reported 2024 at roughly 1.28°C (the record) and 2025 lower (about 1.23–1.24°C, near-tied with 2023), so the binding condition is effectively beating the 2024 record. Background: the year began with weak La Niña conditions, which typically suppress global temperatures in the first half; forecasts issued around the turn of the year (e.g., Met Office-style outlooks) placed 2026 most likely among the top three years with only a minority chance of a new record, contingent on El Niño developing during 2026. A record in 2026 would require a fast-developing, fairly strong El Niño plus persistently elevated ocean heat, similar to the 2023 pattern but from a higher baseline. No 2026 observational data were supplied, so I cannot condition on actual year-to-date anomalies or ENSO state as of September 2026. Reasons the estimate could be too high: if La Niña lingered or El Niño was late/weak, year-to-date anomalies would likely run near 2025 levels and a record would be nearly foreclosed by September; the 1.28 threshold is a demanding El Niño-peak value. Reasons it could be too low: underlying warming (~0.02°C/yr plus possible aerosol/forcing effects) and unusually warm 2023–2025 oceans mean even a moderate El Niño onset could push late-2026 months to record highs; GISS's specific methodology has sometimes run warmer than other datasets, and actual 2026 data (unknown to me) may already show a record-pace year.
limitations: No supplied evidence on 2026 year-to-date temperatures or ENSO status as of the September 2026 cutoff.
Recollection of exact 2024/2025 GISS values may be slightly off; rounding conventions in GISS reporting could matter near the 1.28 threshold.
Estimate relies on general climate-forecast priors rather than current observations.
